title: System of Particles & Rotational Motion
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Center of Mass, Impulse-Momentum Collisions, Moment of Inertia Theorems, Torque, Angular Momentum Conservation, Rolling Motion & Pure Rotation Dynamics
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: From Point Masses to Rigid Bodies

Up to Chapter 05, we mostly treated objects as point masses—ignoring their size and shape. But in the real world, objects like wheels, doors, planets, and spinning tops have extended dimensions and can both translate (move from place to place) and rotate simultaneously.

What Is a Rigid Body?
A Rigid Body is an idealized extended object in which the distance between any two constituent particles remains absolutely fixed and unyielding, no matter what forces are applied to it!

topics.title: Center of Mass (COM), Motion of COM, System of Particles & Collisions
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Center of Mass (COM) Position Formula
Definition:
The Center of Mass is the unique single point where the entire mass of an extended system of particles can be imagined to be concentrated for studying its translational motion under external forces.
$$\text{Discrete Particles (1D):} \quad \boxed{X_{\text{cm}} = \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2 + \dots + m_n x_n}{m_1 + m_2 + \dots + m_n} = \frac{\sum m_i x_i}{\sum m_i}}$$
$$\text{Continuous Bodies (Integration):} \quad \boxed{X_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\int x\,dm}{M}, \qquad Y_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\int y\,dm}{M}, \qquad Z_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\int z\,dm}{M}}$$
1.2 Motion of Center of Mass & Internal Forces
$$\vec{F}_{\text{ext, net}} = M \vec{a}_{\text{cm}} \qquad \left(\text{where } M = \sum m_i \text{ is total mass}\right)$$

Crucial Insight: Internal forces between particles (like internal collisions, explosions, or spring forces) cancel out in pairs by Newton's Third Law. Therefore, internal forces can never change the acceleration or trajectory of the Center of Mass!
topics.derivationHtml:
Standard Result: Center of Mass of a Uniform Semicircular Ring and Disk

1. Semicircular Ring of Radius $R$:
$$Y_{\text{cm}} = \frac{2R}{\pi} \approx 0.637 R$$

2. Semicircular Solid Disk of Radius $R$:
$$Y_{\text{cm}} = \frac{4R}{3\pi} \approx 0.424 R$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (COM Shift when a person walks on a boat): If a person of mass $m$ walks a distance $L$ relative to a boat of mass $M$ floating in still water, the boat shifts backward by distance $\Delta x = \frac{m}{m+M}L$ relative to the ground.

topics.title: Moment of Inertia (MI), Radius of Gyration, Parallel & Perpendicular Axis Theorems
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Definition of Moment of Inertia ($I$) & Radius of Gyration ($k$)
Definition:
Moment of Inertia ($I$) is the rotational analog of mass. It measures how difficult it is to change an object's rotational speed about a given axis.
$$I = \sum m_i r_i^2 = \int r^2\,dm \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Radius of Gyration: } \boxed{k = \sqrt{\frac{I}{M}}}$$
2.2 The Two Great Theorems of Moment of Inertia
TheoremStatement & FormulaValid For
1. Perpendicular Axis Theorem$I_z = I_x + I_y$ (where $x, y, z$ are mutually perpendicular axes meeting at origin).Strictly 2D (Planar) Objects (lamina, ring, disk, flat plate).
2. Parallel Axis Theorem$I_{\text{axis}} = I_{\text{cm}} + M d^2$ ($d =$ distance between parallel axes).Any 2D or 3D Rigid Body of total mass $M$.
2.3 Standard Moment of Inertia Formulae Dictionary
BodyAxisMoment of Inertia ($I$)
Thin Ring / Hollow CylinderThrough center $\perp$ to plane$M R^2$
Thin Ring / Hollow CylinderDiameter / Lengthwise$\frac{1}{2} M R^2$
Solid Disk / Solid CylinderThrough center $\perp$ to plane$\frac{1}{2} M R^2$
Solid Disk / Solid CylinderDiameter$\frac{1}{4} M R^2 + \frac{1}{12} M L^2$
Solid SphereDiameter$\frac{2}{5} M R^2$
Hollow Sphere (Spherical Shell)Diameter$\frac{2}{3} M R^2$
Thin Rod of length $L$Through center $\perp$ to rod$\frac{1}{12} M L^2$
Thin Rod of length $L$Through end $\perp$ to rod$\frac{1}{3} M L^2$
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof of Parallel Axis Theorem

$I_{\text{axis}} = \sum m_i (x_i + d)^2 = \sum m_i x_i^2 + d^2 \sum m_i + 2d \sum m_i x_i$. Since $\sum m_i x_i = 0$ at the COM, $\boxed{I_{\text{axis}} = I_{\text{cm}} + M d^2}$.

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Perpendicular Axis Theorem on 3D Objects): Never apply the Perpendicular Axis Theorem to a solid sphere or solid cylinder—they are 3D objects, not 2D laminae!

topics.title: Torque, Angular Momentum & Conservation of Angular Momentum
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Torque ($\vec{\tau}$) & Angular Momentum ($\vec{L}$)
$$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p} = I\vec{\omega}$$
$$\sum \vec{\tau}_{\text{ext}} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = I\vec{\alpha}$$
3.2 Conservation of Angular Momentum
Master Rule:
If the net external torque acting on a system is zero ($\sum \vec{\tau}_{\text{ext}} = 0$), the total angular momentum of the system remains strictly constant ($I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2 = \text{constant}$).
topics.derivationHtml:
Ice Skater Spin Derivation

When an ice skater pulls her arms inward, her moment of inertia decreases ($I \downarrow$), so her angular speed increases proportionally ($\omega \uparrow$) to keep $L = I\omega$ constant.

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Axis of Angular Momentum): Angular momentum conservation can only be applied about a fixed point or about the Center of Mass of the system.

topics.title: Rolling Motion without Slipping: Kinetic Energy & Acceleration on an Inclined Plane
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Pure Rolling Motion Conditions
Definition:
Pure rolling is a combination of translation of the center of mass with speed $v_{\text{cm}}$ and rotation about the COM with angular speed $\omega$.
$$\textbf{Condition for Pure Rolling (No Slipping at Point of Contact):} \quad \boxed{v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega, \qquad a_{\text{cm}} = R\alpha}$$
$$\textbf{Total Kinetic Energy of Rolling Body:} \quad \boxed{K_{\text{total}} = K_{\text{trans}} + K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}Mv_{\text{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}Mv_{\text{cm}}^2\left(1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}\right)}$$
4.2 Acceleration of Rolling Body Down an Inclined Plane
$$\boxed{a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \boxed{v_{\text{bottom}} = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}}}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Acceleration Down Incline

Apply Newton's laws for translation ($mg\sin\theta - f = Ma$) and rotation ($\tau = fR = I\alpha$). Substituting $I = Mk^2$ and $\alpha = a/R$ yields $a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + k^2/R^2}$.
topics.graphSvg: <svg viewBox='0 0 680 190' style='width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;'><rect width='680' height='190' rx='8' fill='#080b12' stroke='#1e293b'/><circle cx='340' cy='95' r='45' fill='none' stroke='#00f0ff' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='340' cy='95' r='5' fill='#ff0055'/><line x1='280' y1='145' x2='400' y2='145' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='2'/><text x='340' y='170' fill='#00e676' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle'>Pure Rolling: Point of contact is instantaneously at rest (v_contact = 0)</text></svg>
topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Which shape reaches bottom first?): A solid sphere ($k^2/R^2 = 2/5 = 0.4$) always reaches the bottom of an incline faster than a ring ($k^2/R^2 = 1$) because its rotational inertia is smaller, so more energy goes into translation!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 06: System of Particles & Rotational Motion!
summary:
• COM: $X_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\sum m_i x_i}{\sum m_i}$.
  • Theorems: $I_z = I_x + I_y$, $\; I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2$.
  • Rolling: $v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega$, $\; K = \frac{1}{2}Mv^2(1 + k^2/R^2)$.

questions.prompt: Find the moment of inertia of a uniform circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about a tangent in its own plane.
questions.explanation: MI about a diameter is $I_{\text{diam}} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$. Using the parallel axis theorem with distance $d = R$: $I_{\text{tangent}} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2 + MR^2 = \frac{3}{2}MR^2$.

questions.prompt: A solid sphere, a hollow sphere, a solid cylinder, and a ring of the same mass and radius are released from rest at the top of an inclined plane. Which one reaches the bottom first?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is $a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + k^2/R^2}$. The solid sphere has the smallest $k^2/R^2$ ($2/5 = 0.4$), giving it the highest acceleration and shortest time to reach the bottom.
